articles.title: DocuMorph: Living 3D Architecture Constellations & Interactive API Sandboxes
articles.excerpt: 🧬 DocuMorph: Living 3D Architecture Constellations & Interactive API Sandboxes Every engineering team knows the dread of documentation drift: you design an architecture diagram, write API specificati…
articles.body: 🧬 DocuMorph: Living 3D Architecture Constellations & Interactive API Sandboxes Every engineering team knows the dread of documentation drift : you design an architecture diagram, write API specifications, and within three weeks the code evolves while the documentation quietly rots. Architecture diagrams in Confluence or Eraser stay static, while developers scramble across Swagger tabs and Postman collections just to see if an endpoint actually behaves the way the docs claim. DocuMorph was built to solve this once and for all: transforming raw code, GitHub links, and API specifications into living, interactive documentation with dual 2D/3D WebGL architecture constellations and an executable API sandbox directly on the canvas. 🌟 The Core Innovations 1.

articles.body: Before touching a thumbnail pipeline that shrinks cut-out PNGs, I wanted to know one thing: does it matter whether RGB is premultiplied by alpha before the resize? This post uses two of my three test cut-outs, the portrait and a white dog, and covers what they settled and what they left open. The cut-outs came from ImgIng https://imging.ai/ in a desktop browser, using its AI cut-out tool and exporting PNG at the input size. The sources are two Wikimedia Commons photos, a portrait (Dmitry Makeev, CC BY-SA 4.0) and a Bichon Frise (TudorTulok, CC BY-SA 4.0), both scaled to a 2000 px long edge. I shrank each result by a factor F and enlarged it back, once per channel and once premultiplied. Everything below is these two images, one Apple M4, one run each.

articles.title: Ensure Family Data Access After Owner's Death: Implement Shared Credentials or Automated Backup Solutions
articles.excerpt: Introduction: The Silent Threat of Inaccessible Self-Hosted Data Consider a scenario where a self-hosted server, humming quietly in a home office, stores a lifetime of personal data—family photos, leg…
articles.body: Introduction: The Silent Threat of Inaccessible Self-Hosted Data Consider a scenario where a self-hosted server, humming quietly in a home office, stores a lifetime of personal data—family photos, legal documents, and digital archives. Upon the owner’s death, this server transforms from a repository of memories into an inaccessible vault. Without documented credentials, technical documentation, or a clear succession plan, non-technical family members face an insurmountable barrier. This is not a speculative risk but a documented reality, as evidenced by cases where irreplaceable data has been lost due to the absence of a structured handover mechanism.
articles.author: Elena Burtseva

articles.title: Necro-Shell: An Adversarial, LLM-Powered Haunted Terminal
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine Necro-Shell is a terminal wrapper designed to transform the sterile, logical environment of a command-l…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built Necro-Shell is a terminal wrapper designed to transform the sterile, logical environment of a command-line interface into a psychological horror experience. Instead of a traditional shell that simply executes commands silently, Necro-Shell acts as an eerie "witness." It uses a local, open-weight Large Language Model to monitor your command inputs, interpret your intent, and "whisper" unsettling, context-aware commentary back to you before executing the task. If you delete files ( rm ), it mourns them. If you navigate directories ( cd ), it asks what you are running from. If you seek administrative privileges ( sudo ), it mocks your hubris.

articles.title: DMARC passes SPF and DKIM but still fails? Check alignment
articles.excerpt: A common surprise: your mail shows spf=pass and dkim=pass in the headers, yet DMARC reports fail. The cause is almost always alignment. DMARC does not just need SPF or DKIM to pass. It needs one of th…
articles.body: A common surprise: your mail shows spf=pass and dkim=pass in the headers, yet DMARC reports fail . The cause is almost always alignment. What DMARC actually checks DMARC does not just need SPF or DKIM to pass. It needs one of them to pass for a domain that matches the visible From address . SPF is checked against the envelope sender (Return-Path), not the From header. DKIM is checked against the d= domain in the signature. If a third-party sender uses its own Return-Path domain and its own d= domain, both checks can pass and neither will align with your From domain. Find it in 2 minutes Send a test message to a mailbox you control, open "Show original" and read Authentication-Results .
articles.author: Mogley1011

articles.title: n8n vs Zapier: Which Zaps Break When You Move to Self-Hosted n8n with Docker, and How Much Work Is Rebuilding Them?
articles.excerpt: Treat a move from Zapier to self-hosted n8n as a rebuild, not a migration, because n8n has no native importer for Zaps. Simple webhook and API Zaps usually transfer cleanly. The ones that cause troubl…
articles.body: Treat a move from Zapier to self-hosted n8n as a rebuild, not a migration, because n8n has no native importer for Zaps. Simple webhook and API Zaps usually transfer cleanly. The ones that cause trouble depend on apps with no native n8n node, Zapier-hosted features such as Tables or Interfaces, or OAuth connections you must now register yourself. Audit your Zaps by those three risks before you commit, because that list, not your Zap count, determines the workload. TL;DR Solo operator with a handful of linear Zaps, such as a freelancer sending form leads to a CRM: Migrate first, because mainstream apps and short workflows are the cheapest kind to rebuild.

articles.title: Googlebot Saw Empty Tables on Our JavaScript Site: What We Found in Search Console
articles.excerpt: Our site is a set of market-data tools: screeners, heatmaps and calculators. Tables are filled by JavaScript from a small backend endpoint. For months Search Console showed "Crawled - currently not in…
articles.body: Our site is a set of market-data tools: screeners, heatmaps and calculators. Tables are filled by JavaScript from a small backend endpoint. For months Search Console showed "Crawled - currently not indexed" for almost every tool page, and we blamed content quality. Then we looked at two reports we had never opened, and found two plain technical bugs. This post is from the Vunelix team and the site in question is ours. The lessons apply to any JavaScript-rendered site. Bug 1: 96% of Googlebot's requests went to one endpoint that always failed In Search Console, open Settings → Crawl stats → By response . Ours showed about 7.8 million Googlebot requests in 90 days, and 96% of them were "Other client error (4XX)".

The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. articles.body: Our time on our "space mission" underwater was coming to an end, and I felt like what I imagine an astronaut on the International Space Station (ISS) must feel before returning to Earth. On one hand, you are excited to return to your home and loved ones, as well as to fresh food and normal hygiene. On the other, you know you will miss your crew and the incredible experience of being in space. While my SEA STAR crew and I had not left Earth during our mission, we were separated from the surface of our home planet for five days. All we saw was a green alien water world surrounding us. We did this to live and work like astronauts on the ISS .

articles.title: India launches next-gen navigation satellite to orbit (video)
articles.excerpt: India launched the NVS-03 navigation satellite to orbit today (Oct. 30) atop a GSLV rocket. It was the fourth orbital launch from Indian soil so far this year.
articles.body: India bolstered its homegrown satellite-navigation system today (Oct. 30). A GSLV Mark II rocket launched the nation's NVS-03 satellite from Satish Dhawan Space Centre today at 2:21 p.m. EDT (1821 GMT and 11:51 p.m. India Standard Time). Everything went well: The rocket deployed NVS-03 into geostationary transfer orbit as planned, officials with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) announced on X about 30 minutes after liftoff. An Indian GSLV Mark II rocket launches the NVS-03 navigation satellite on Oct. 30, 2026. (Image credit: ISRO) NVS-03 is the third next-gen satellite that India has launched for the Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC), its version of the United States' Global Positioning System ( GPS ).

articles.title: 5 horror franchises that went to space... and one that absolutely should have but didn't
articles.excerpt: In space, no one can hear you scream, a bit like the empty theater screens that some horror franchise's final installments limp. But there are still some real gems among the space-based frightfests.
articles.body: In space, no one can hear you scream... not unlike in the empty theater screens that aging horror franchises play to when the lustre has gone and their final installments limp to the public. It is perhaps little wonder that some horror franchises go to space to die... or take long breaks, at least. In celebration of Halloween , we're running down some horror franchises that made the journey to the final frontier, resulting in films that range from the sublime and outrageously campy fun to just pure awful. Absent from the list are space horror movies that have space baked into their natural fabric. So no Event Horizon, no Alien, and no Critters 4 (they were aliens, so they just went back to space; that doesn't count). 1.
